final_text: Rosamond Oliver kept her word about visiting me. She usually called at the school during her morning ride. She would canter up to the door on her pony, followed by a mounted servant in livery. Nothing more exquisite than her appearance could be imagined, in her purple riding habit with her black velvet riding cap set gracefully above the long curls that brushed her cheek and floated to her shoulders: and this is how she would enter the rustic building and glide through the dazzled ranks of village children. She generally came at the hour when Mr. Rivers was giving his daily lesson in religious instruction. Her gaze, I fear, pierced the young clergyman's heart to the quick. A kind of instinct seemed to warn him of her entrance, even when he was not looking; and when he was looking quite away from the door, if she appeared at it, his cheek would glow, and his marble-like features, though they refused to relax, changed in some indescribable way and, in their very stillness, became expressive of a repressed passion stronger than any flexing muscle or darting glance could show.

problem: Source "She had been indulged from her birth, but was not absolutely spoilt" is reversed: modern says she "had been spoiled since birth, but was not ruined by it".
final_text: Miss Oliver had already honored me with frequent visits to my cottage. I had come to know her whole character, which had no mystery or pretense: she was flirtatious but not heartless; demanding, but not worthlessly selfish. She had been indulged since birth, but was not completely spoiled. She was impulsive but good-natured; vain (she could not help it, when every glance in the mirror showed her such a flood of loveliness) but not affected; generous; free of the arrogance of wealth; straightforward; reasonably intelligent; cheerful, lively, and carefree: she was very charming, in short, even to a cool female observer like me; but she was not deeply interesting or truly impressive. Her mind was of a very different sort from that of St. John's sisters, for instance. Still, I liked her almost as much as I liked my former pupil Adèle; except that for a child we have watched over and taught, a closer affection develops than we can give an equally appealing adult acquaintance.

problem: The biblical allusion "Mammon" is flattened to "greed"; the instructions ask for allusions to stay recognizable.
final_text: "I have come to see how you are spending your holiday," he said. "Not in gloomy thought, I hope? No, that is good: while you draw you will not feel lonely. You see, I still worry about you, though you have held up wonderfully so far. I have brought you a book for the evening," and he laid on the table a new publication—a poem: one of those genuine masterworks so often granted to the fortunate public of those days—the golden age of modern literature. Alas! the readers of our time are less blessed. But take heart! I will not stop to accuse or lament. I know poetry is not dead, nor genius lost; nor has Mammon—the god of money—gained power over either, to bind or destroy them: they will both assert their existence, their presence, their freedom and their strength again one day. Mighty angels, safe in heaven! They smile when base souls triumph and timid ones weep over their destruction. Poetry destroyed? Genius banished? No! Mediocrity—no: do not let envy suggest that thought. No; they not only survive but reign and redeem: and without their divine influence everywhere, you would live in hell—the hell of your own smallness.

final_text: I said first, "Take a seat, Mr. Rivers." But he answered, as he always did, that he could not stay. "Very well," I responded mentally, "stand if you like; but you shall not leave just yet, I am determined. Solitude is at least as harmful for you as it is for me. I will see if I can find the secret spring of your confidence, and an opening in that marble chest through which I can pour one drop of the balm of sympathy."

final_text: He continued to gaze at the picture: the longer he looked, the more firmly he held it, the more he seemed to want it. "It is like her!" he murmured; "the eye is perfectly done: the color, light, expression are perfect. It smiles!"

final_text: "Now," he said, "that little space was given over to fever and fantasy. I rested my head on the breast of temptation and willingly placed my neck under her yoke of flowers; I tasted her cup. The pillow was burning: there is a serpent in the garland: the wine has a bitter taste: her promises are hollow—her offers false. I see and know all this."

problem: Source "deistic philosophers" becomes "godless philosophers"; deists believe in God (but not revelation), so "godless" changes the contrast St. John draws ("I believe the Gospel").
final_text: "No. There is this difference between me and deist philosophers, who believe in God but not in revelation: I believe; and I believe the Gospel. You chose the wrong word. I am not a pagan but a Christian philosopher—a follower of the faith of Jesus. As His disciple I embrace His pure, merciful, generous teachings. I champion them: I am sworn to spread them. Won over to religion in my youth, she has cultivated my original qualities like this: from the tiny seed of natural affection, she has grown the towering tree of love for humanity. From the wild, stringy root of human integrity, she has raised a proper sense of divine justice. The ambition to win power and fame for my wretched self, she has transformed into the ambition to expand my Master's kingdom; to win victories for the banner of the cross. This is what religion has done for me; making the best use of the raw material; pruning and training nature. But she could not root out nature: nor will nature be rooted out until this mortal puts on immortality."

final_text: "Half an hour ago," he went on, "I mentioned my impatience to hear the rest of a story. On reflection, I think the matter will be better handled if I take the narrator's part and make you the listener. Before I begin, it is only fair to warn you that the story will sound rather familiar to your ears; but stale details often gain a certain freshness when they pass through new lips. For the rest, whether familiar or new, it is short.

final_text: I went cold with dread: my worst fears were probably true. He had in all likelihood left England and rushed in reckless desperation to some former haunt on the Continent. And what opiate for his terrible suffering—what outlet for his strong passions—had he sought there? I dared not answer the question. Oh, my poor master—once almost my husband—whom I had so often called "my dear Edward!"

final_text: I need not describe in detail the further battles I fought and arguments I used to get the inheritance settled as I wished. My task was very difficult; but as I was absolutely resolved—as my cousins eventually saw that my mind was truly and unshakably fixed on making a fair division of the property—as they must in their own hearts have felt the justice of the intention, and must, besides, have known instinctively that in my place they would have done exactly what I wished to do—they yielded at last so far as to agree to put the matter to arbitration. The judges chosen were Mr. Oliver and a skilled lawyer: both agreed with my view. I got my way. The legal documents were drawn up: St. John, Diana, Mary, and I each came into a comfortable, independent income.
